thread.title: Cramer: What's Your Plan for This Week's Earnings Gauntlet?

title: Cramer: What's Your Plan for This Week's Earnings Gauntlet?
text:
Cramer: What's Your Plan for This Week's Earnings Gauntlet? By jpm 
Can you trade 'em. Can you get in and out? Can you use the weakness to take a swing? Or do you recognize that we are up so much that it's not too late to take a profit. 
All of these thoughts swirl through our heads on a down day after so many strong ones and they are front and center ideas for certain. 
Let me give you my take. 
First, if you have been waiting for a break to get in for your contributions, whether they are for retirement or college savings or anything long-term then this is your time. You have a week of earnings that is so important that it's literally a gauntlet. It will be gotten through but not without damage. That damage is your chance. 
So what I would do is use the weakness to put money in an index fund. If you want to be really granular, I would actually do a little each day because we don't know how things are going to play out but the dip must be used to apply those funds. 
I like the term apply because it is clinical, not emotional. 
More than 100 S&P companies report this week and we've had a straight up market. I do not think the odds favor a continuation if only because we are far more vulnerable to a letdown now than we were with the full heard of steam we came into today's market with. 
So, apply away, a little each day. If you have $2,000 to put to work, I would put half of it to work this week. Then wait to see what happens. 
Notice I am not even discussing taking money out for retirement. Remember my long-standing view. We have a mass of baby boomers who grew up thinking that if you are still going to contribute to retirement you have to re-arrange your funds and be far more fixed income including cash. 
To me that's just wrong. If you live to the eighties or nineties you will not be earning enough switching big to bonds. That's why I am not even including them into the mix for most readers. Good quality stocks with nice and growing dividends that can be reinvested makes for the most prudent allocation and the S&P 500 provides just that. I don't care how you buy it. I think a low-cost fund is the way to go. 
Some would say with the ten year US treasury now at 2.70 that's good competition to stocks and should be part of the mix. I say, later, later. Not yet. There will come a time when a risk free yield will have a place beyond the oldest of viewers. I still think it's crummy competition vs. an index fund. 
Now how about individual stocks? Okay, this is something that has to be taken head on especially because I think the market might have a tilt down this week. 
Let's start with Apple ( AAPL ) , the elephant in the room. This Thursday the largest company on Earth reports and I am indifferent to the quarter. I know, that sounds like the equivalent of punting on fourth and two, betting that the defense can stop the bears and you get the ball back. 
But let me tell you why I have this position. First, I think, in some ways, Apple has been set up to fail. So many analysts have insisted on saying that Apple's got a supercycle going on between the 8 and the X. All I can tell you is a supercycle designation is like the old Sports Illustrated curse. That's where an athlete peaked when he or she was on the cover of the magazine. 
That superstition seems to have fallen by the wayside. But the supercycle curse is very much with us because the last three supercycle designations were coal going into the brutal 2011 collapse and the oil drilling and fracking sand supercycles of 2014. Some of these were brought about by their own hands. Peabody, the largest coal company would talk to anyone about the coal supercycle. The rest of the coal companies were equally as bullish, bullish that is before they all collapsed with worldwide coal pricing.pst 
But the fracking sand and oil supercycles were all about oil going through the roof. A few months after the supercycle became the parlance, and the participants embraced it, oil went through the floor. 
Apple to its ever-lasting credit NEVER used the supercycle term. Never. That was a figment of the research firms that I think were really what I call faux bulls all along and it set up Apple to fail when it has to give guidance that is not up to supercycle standards, whatever the heck they are. 
The faux bulls want to turn bears by saying, "you know how you thought the stock was cheap? Well we are slicing numbers and now against the new, lowered numbers, the stock's expensive." 
Me? I know better. I never thought there would be a supercycle. I do think there are a series of better and better phones that appeal to those tens of millions who are loyal to the ecosystem. I recall how analysts got all bulled up in 2015 about the stock in the 130s and then they fled it like the plague when it hit $93. 
I don't know what Apple will say. I don't know what they will report. I just don't want people to flee and then not get back in when it turns out there's plenty of legs to the new products and the service stream is huge. 
Does the stock have a bad feel? No kidding, yes. Can it go down? What the heck. It's a stock for heaven's sake. But it's a long, multi-year season and that's how I look at it. 
Sure, I want every stock including Apple to be Netflix ( NFLX ) , the one that won't quit because it turns out the company itself is worth a heck of lot more than we thought because the total addressable market is much bigger than we thought. But that's been the rarity, one that seems to be shared by Amazon.com ( AMZN ) , which, like Netflix ran right into the quarter and, I believe, like Netflix, will run after the quarter, too, as new huge forms of revenue, this time from advertising, augment retail and web services sales. 
Unlike Amazon and Netflix, Apple has a whole ecosystem of stocks that go down with it, particularly the parts makers. No need to buy until you see the whites of Apple's eyes. 
How about the cyclical stocks that are giving up so much ground today? I like them. They are multi-year stories that historically ebb and flow. This time, though, they have a synchronized global economy in their favor, something that we know continues to put pressure on our interest rates, something I am certain will come up when the Fed convenes for Janet Yellen's hurrah. What a great job she did. She kept us in the straight and narrow low-rate cause until business picked up in a safe way, augmented, hate em or like em, from President Trump's pro-growth anti-regulation, pro-stock policies. 
Oils? Let em come in. We think oil's resting. 
Drugs? We need more down days to shake out the sunshine patriots, kind of like what happened with the biotechs before they caught fire and are now the strongest group in the market. 
Banks? With rates going higher they are best in show. You have to hope for the unthinkable, that Apple's guidance is so weak that it pulls down everything. If that's the case, this group, led by JP Morgan ( JPM ) is the best place to buy because they are cheap and will remain that way until they move well up from where they sit now. 
So, be ready for volatility. Understand that you can trade some of the big techs all you want. My take? Own them, don't trade them, but understand that you may lose before you win again.
